newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FAA seeks $300 million in new user fees.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FAA seeks $300 million in new user fees.

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration said on Tuesday it hoped to raise $300 million next year through new user fees on small turbine aircraft, on international cargo and for the cost of airport security.

Barry Valentine, the FAA's acting administrator, said the new user fees would be temporary until a national review commission completed work and recommended how best to meet the agency's long-term financial needs.
Valentine did not break down the revenue from each user fee, except to say they would be based on the FAA services required by the aircraft or aviation operation.

He told the House of Representatives Appropriations aviation subcommmittee that the specific funding legislation would be submitted to Congress shortly to be included in the agency's budget request for the 1998 fiscal year.
The Air Transport Association, the trade group of major U.S. carriers, had no immediate comment on the cargo or security user fees.
But the new fee on turbine engine planes met opposition from the General Aircraft Manufacturers Association, whose members make smaller commuter airliners and planes for corporate and private use.
It said that if the FAA needed additional funds it should increase the existing fuel tax, which would be more equitable and easier to collect.

Valentine also told the subcommittee that an overflight fee -- charges to foreign planes that overfly U.S. terrirtory -- would go into effect in about two months and would raise about $100 million a year.
He said the agency's aim was to reach 100 percent user funding in fiscal 1999 through a system of fees that would charge users for the aviation services they required.
The National Civil Aviation Review Commission is to consider the most equitable long-term funding for the FAA and to make its recommendations by next summer.
A major part of its review is how to fairly assess users of the air system the fees that are needed to operate it.
Major airlines want to scrap the current method of an airline tax based on ticket price, saying it penalized the carriers that fly long distances and charge high fares, but use fewer FAA services.
With the flat tax, they said, they subsidize low-cost carriers who fly frequent point-to-point services.

But the low-cost carriers, such as Southwest, say their flights take less air traffic controller time than the big carriers with their hub and spoke operations which often have many planes landing and taking off at the same time.
